title: IUPAC Classification and Periodic Trends
topicTitle: IUPAC classification and periodic trends: atomic radii, ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic characters and anomalies
notes: ### 1. Atomic and Ionic Radii
• **Covalent Radius:** Half the inter-nuclear distance between two identical non-metallic atoms bonded by a single covalent bond ($r_{cov} = d/2$).

• **Van der Waals Radius:** Half the distance between nuclei of two non-bonded adjacent identical atoms of separate molecules in solid state. Order: $r_{vdw} > r_{metallic} > r_{covalent}$. Noble gases are reported only in Van der Waals radius, which is why noble gas radii appear anomalously large.
• **Periodic Trend:**
- **Across a Period (Left to Right):** Atomic radius decreases steadily due to increasing effective nuclear charge ($Z_{eff} = Z - \sigma$), which pulls electrons closer without adding new shells.
- **Down a Group (Top to Bottom):** Atomic radius increases because new principal energy shells ($n$) are added, which outweighs the increase in nuclear charge.
• **Ionic Radius Rules:**
- **Cation < Parent Atom:** Removal of valence electrons decreases electron-electron repulsion and increases $Z_{eff}$ per electron (e.g., $Na^+ = 102$ pm < $Na = 186$ pm).
- **Anion > Parent Atom:** Addition of electrons increases mutual electron repulsion, swelling the electron cloud ($Cl^- = 181$ pm > $Cl = 99$ pm).

- **Isoelectronic Series:** Species with identical number of electrons (e.g., $N^{3-}, O^{2-}, F^-, Na^+, Mg^{2+}, Al^{3+}$ each have 10 electrons). As nuclear charge (protons) increases, radius decreases strictly:
### 2. Ionization Enthalpy (IE) & Critical Anomalies

• **Definition:** The minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state: $X(g) + \Delta_i H \rightarrow X^+(g) + e^-$. Units: kJ/mol or eV/atom.

• **Successive Ionization Enthalpies:** $\Delta_i H_3 > \Delta_i H_2 > \Delta_i H_1$ always, because removing an electron from a positively charged cation experiences much higher electrostatic attraction.
• **General Trend:** Increases across a period (increasing $Z_{eff}$), decreases down a group (increasing atomic size and shielding).
• **High-Yield NEB Exam Anomalies:**

1. **Beryllium vs Boron:** $IE_1(Be) > IE_1(B)$ ($899$ vs $801$ kJ/mol). Beryllium ($1s^2 2s^2$) has a completely filled 2s subshell with greater penetration power and screening, whereas Boron ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$) has a solitary 2p electron in a higher energy subshell that is easier to remove.

2. **Nitrogen vs Oxygen:** $IE_1(N) > IE_1(O)$ ($1402$ vs $1314$ kJ/mol). Nitrogen ($1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1$) possesses an extra-stable half-filled 2p subshell with maximum exchange energy. Oxygen ($1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1$) has a paired electron in the $2p_x$ orbital; inter-electronic pairing repulsion makes this fourth electron easier to remove.
3. **Magnesium vs Aluminium:** $IE_1(Mg) > IE_1(Al)$ ($737$ vs $577$ kJ/mol) for identical subshell penetration reasons ($3s^2$ vs $3s^2 3p^1$).
4. **Phosphorus vs Sulfur:** $IE_1(P) > IE_1(S)$ ($1012$ vs $1000$ kJ/mol) due to half-filled $3p^3$ configuration in phosphorus.
### 3. Electron Gain Enthalpy (Electron Affinity, $\Delta_{eg}H$)

• **Definition:** Enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom to form a monovalent anion: $X(g) + e^- \rightarrow X^-(g)$. Usually negative (exothermic) for first electron addition (except noble gases and Be/Mg/N where it is positive/endothermic).

• **Second Electron Gain Enthalpy:** Always strongly POSITIVE (endothermic, e.g., $O^-(g) + e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}(g)$, $\Delta_{eg}H = +780$ kJ/mol) because incoming electron must overcome strong electrostatic repulsion from the negatively charged anion.
• **Crucial Group 17 Exception (Cl vs F):**
- Experimental negative electron gain enthalpy order: **$Cl > F > Br > I$** (Cl = -349 kJ/mol, F = -328 kJ/mol).

- **Reason:** Fluorine atom has an exceptionally small and compact 2p subshell ($n=2$). When an extra electron approaches, it suffers high inter-electronic repulsion from the tightly packed valence electrons. Chlorine has a more spacious 3p subshell ($n=3$), which accommodates the extra electron with significantly less repulsion.
• **Crucial Group 16 Exception (S vs O):** Sulfur has higher electron affinity than Oxygen for the exact same reason ($S = -200$ kJ/mol, $O = -141$ kJ/mol).
### 4. Electronegativity (EN)
• **Definition:** The qualitative relative tendency of an atom in a chemical compound to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself.

• **Pauling Scale (Most common):** Based on excess bond energies. Values: Fluorine (F = 4.0, highest in periodic table), Oxygen (O = 3.5), Nitrogen (N = 3.0), Chlorine (Cl = 3.0), Bromine (Br = 2.8), Carbon (C = 2.5), Hydrogen (H = 2.1), Cesium/Francium (Cs/Fr = 0.7, lowest).
• **Mulliken-Jaffe Scale:** Average of ionization energy and electron affinity: $EN = (IE + EA) / 2$ (in eV).
• **Factors Affecting Electronegativity:**
- Oxidation State: Higher oxidation state element is more electronegative ($Fe^{3+} > Fe^{2+}, Sn^{4+} > Sn^{2+}$).
- Hybridization: Higher % s-character = higher EN ($sp$ [50% s] > $sp^2$ [33.3% s] > $sp^3$ [25% s]). Thus, terminal alkynes are acidic.
### 5. Metallic, Non-Metallic, and Chemical Reactivity Trends
• **Metallic Character (Electropositivity):** Decreases across a period (electrons harder to lose), increases down a group. Most metallic: Francium/Cesium; Most non-metallic: Fluorine.
• **Nature of Oxides:**
- Basic oxides: Group 1 and 2 metal oxides ($Na_2O, K_2O, CaO, BaO$).
- Amphoteric oxides: React with both acids and bases ($Al_2O_3, ZnO, BeO, PbO, SnO_2$).
$ZnO + 2HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_2 + H_2O$
$ZnO + 2NaOH + H_2O \rightarrow Na_2[Zn(OH)_4]$ (Sodium zincate)
$Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH + 3H_2O \rightarrow 2Na[Al(OH)_4]$ (Sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate)
- Acidic oxides: Non-metal oxides ($SO_2, SO_3, N_2O_5, P_4O_{10}, Cl_2O_7$) and transition metals in high oxidation states ($CrO_3, Mn_2O_7$).
- Neutral oxides: Do not react with acids or bases ($CO, NO, N_2O$).
• **Diagonal Relationship Causes:** Identical charge-to-radius ratio (polarizing power $\phi = \text{charge}/\text{radius}$). Pairs: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si.
confusion: ❌ Noble gases have zero atomic radius because they do not bond. ✅ Noble gases have non-bonded Van der Waals radii, which are physically larger than covalent radii of neighboring halogens.

❌ Second electron gain enthalpy of Oxygen ($O^- + e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}$) is negative because $O^{2-}$ gets stable octet. ✅ It is strongly POSITIVE (+780 kJ/mol) because the incoming electron experiences strong repulsive force from the negative $O^-$ ion.

❌ Nitrogen has lower electronegativity than Oxygen, so its ionization enthalpy must be lower. ✅ Electronegativity is for bonded atoms; ionization enthalpy is for isolated gaseous atoms. Nitrogen's half-filled $2p^3$ subshell makes its $IE_1$ higher than Oxygen's.

❌ Fluorine is the most electronegative, so it must have the highest electron gain enthalpy. ✅ Chlorine has the highest negative electron gain enthalpy because Fluorine has compact 2p orbitals causing severe electronic repulsion.
❌ Amphoteric oxides only react with strong acids. ✅ Amphoteric oxides ($Al_2O_3, ZnO, BeO$) react with BOTH strong acids (forming salts) AND strong bases (forming complex aluminates/zincates).

universalFacts: Chlorine has the highest negative electron gain enthalpy (-349 kJ/mol) of any element in the periodic table, while Fluorine is the most electronegative (4.0).
All cations are smaller than their parent atoms; all anions are larger than their parent atoms.
Second and higher electron gain enthalpies are always endothermic (positive) due to electrostatic repulsion from the existing anion.
